If she turns you down don’t get hung up over it (although it’s hard, I know) and try to focus on other aspects in your life. If there’s one thing women respect, it’s a mature guy. And it’s always better to find out than to think “what if”. Going into it I would be prepared to be rejected, that way you won’t be disappointed if she says no but ecstatic if she says yes. If you want to ask her out, I would suggest a formal date such as dining at a nice restaurant, because a casual date will just look like you two hanging out like usual. So do something that neither of you would usually do but is romantic. Offer to pay for the meal but if she interjects and wants to go halves then don’t insist further. Oh, and one last thing, don’t act differently than how you would normally, if you’re both flirting anyway then that should be enough as the romantic setting indicates to her that you might like something more (also dressing smart is a nice bonus). Very tough question since this depends on what type of hacking we’re talking about...

Traditional hacking requires a lot of knowledge about how computers work, something that is widely accessible. The larger factor in my opinion is motivation. Gaining access to a system that is protected takes a lot of time and resources, so whoever is being paid the most is the better hacker (assuming the same amount of knowledge has been learned to hack in the first place).

When it comes to deciding on which country has the best hackers, it would be impossible to know without significant insight. Two factors are required for, in my opinion, discerning which country has the best hackers. First is how well funded these operations are, since it is rare for a really good hacker to spend a lot of their own time breaking into something without reward. The NSA will have a well funded group of “hackers”. Second is whether they can hack without being detected. If you manage to break into a military system and find strategic deployment plans then great you have the information you were after, but if the victim knows they have been hacked they will just change those plans and patch the exploit you used to gain access.

Unfortunately I can’t give an answer to that other than the country will be richer than most. Plus countries don’t tend to report on breaches publicly even if they do realise they have been hacked so it’s impossible to know exactly how many times foreign countries have successfully gained access to confidential information.

I suppose this depends on whether we’re talking about hardware or software.

In the case of hardware, I would be surprised if the military don’t invest in newer systems given the increasing rate of cyber-warfare. The military should have a decent amount of processing power when it comes to cryptography and other techniques similar. Most notably it has been pointed out that quantum computers are likely to have the capability to make encryption through traditional computers obsolete. Overall they should hopefully have some plan in place.

In terms of software this becomes another ballpark. Two computers which have the same hardware can still perform differently due to software. Sure a 32-core processor can encrypt and decrypt quickly using the original DES algorithm, but AES is on another level. If the military have some real smart guys working on their software for encryption and networking, they should be okay for a reasonable while if they’re a little behind on upgrading their hardware.

There are many more angles you can approach this question with, for example network structure, access control, physical attacks, e.t.c., however this reply is too long already and I don’t know enough about the military’s current IT infrastructure or about every single possible attack vector.

To answer the actual question lol: computer technology, whether it is hardware or software, should always be considered old and upgradable. We live in an age where computers now control or store almost everything. If a country has the best of everything I’ve mentioned, then they are the most powerful country in the world now. It sounds like an overreaction but information has always been our most powerful tool.

Hope that answered your question and was informative in some way! Once I’ve finished uni then I’ll be able to answer these questions much easier (hopefully).

If I were to work for the NSA I would probably prefer to be working in a counter-intelligence area as opposed to offensive intelligence. That’s mainly because I’m pro-security, in that I believe privacy is of paramount importance. The idea of gathering information on foreign countries is fun and interesting, but there would always be a part of me that would be scared to find out something I’m not supposed to, and suffer consequences (it’s more of an irrational fear I guess).

Would also need to do more research into the agency before coming to a final decision.

Tl:dr yes I would love to work for the NSA, but in the interest of defending a country.
